comment: Engineering budgets, enforced the way retrieval quality gates are.
Exceeding one is a trade to record in the pull request, not drift to accept.
Only deterministic metrics are gated. Build times are reported, not gated:
shared CI runners vary too much for wall-clock timing to be a reliable
failure signal, and a flaky gate teaches people to ignore gates.
Baseline measured 2026-09-07 on the full dependency set:
binary 39.6 MB, 434 dependencies, cold build 111 s, target/ 2.0 GB.
Re-measured after the store moved to sqlx and dropped tokio-postgres and
refinery: 388 dependencies, target/ 2.7 GB. The gated limits are unchanged,
because a limit that follows every measurement down stops being a limit.
binary_bytes is the executable alone. distribution_bytes adds the native
libraries that ship beside it -- today the retrieval engine, 36.9 MB, which
is linked dynamically and copied next to the binary. That is what a user
actually downloads, so it is what any comparison against a different engine
has to be made against; the executable on its own understates it by more
than its own size.
Gated limits carry roughly 20% headroom over that, which is enough for
ordinary growth and tight enough that a new heavyweight dependency shows up.
The cold build and target size are the real costs of this stack, and they
are one-time rather than per-edit: editing any workspace crate rechecks the
whole workspace in under a second, because the heavy dependencies live
behind a crate boundary and do not rebuild.
